newsitem.title: FRANCE: Cunningham pledges to crack down on beef fraudsters.
newsitem.headline: Cunningham pledges to crack down on beef fraudsters.

text.p: British Agriculture Minister Jack Cunningham, pursuing Labour's dialogue with Europe, said on Tuesday that Britain will tighten controls on illegal beef exports and crack down on fraudsters.

Earlier this month, the European Commission announced that 1,650 tonnes of beef had been exported from Britain to EU countries and nations outside the bloc, despite a ban imposed because of the mad cow crisis.
The beef was fraudulently declared to be of Belgian origin.
"We will simply not tolerate anyone breaking EU law," Cunningham told the European Parliament's special committee monitoring the mad cow crisis.

In striking contrast to his Conservative predecessor Douglas Hogg, who had refused to appear before the committee, Cunningham pledged full cooperation while being grilled by Euro MPs over inadequate controls.
But he cautioned that stronger laws would not guarantee that beef criminals would be stopped.
"We are looking at a very sophisticated international fraud which has gone way beyond the EU," he said.
On Monday, Britain announced that it had closed two meat plants after EU and British investigations showed they were suspected of breaking the worldwide beef export ban.
Asked by reporters if this was the tip of the iceberg, Cunningham replied: "Not that I am aware of."

The EU banned British beef exports in March, 1996, after London admitted that people eating beef infected with Bovine Spongiform Encephalopathy (BSE), or mad cow disease, could catch a fatal brain illness, Creutzfeldt Jacob Disease (CJD).

Cunningham said he strongly supported a European Commission proposal, based on scientific advice, to remove risky animal tissue -- brains, eyes and spinal cords of cattle sheep and goats -- from human and animal food.

He reiterated a warning that if EU farm ministers next week fail to agree the measure then Britain will ensure that beef imports comply with rigorous British food safety standards requiring that the risky parts be removed.
But he stressed that this was not the same thing as a ban.

Cunningham claimed that Britain had made solid progress was being made in implementing a selective cull of animals most at risk to BSE, one of five pre-conditions agreed at an EU summit in Florence in June, 1996, for lifting the ban
The cull was nearly completed in Northern Ireland and in the rest of the United Kingdom, half the 20,000 animals identified to be at risk had been slaughtered.

On ending the crippling export ban, Cunningham said he favoured a ''stepwise'' approach as various regions fulfilled the conditions but added that some of his ministerial colleagues needed to be convinced.
Northern Ireland, which has operated a computerised cattle tracking system for the past nine years, would benefit first.
Cunningham added that computerised system for tracking cattle movements proposed by the EU would be introduced in other parts of the United Kingdom in early 1998.
